course.title: Geometry
course.description: Geometry is the branch of mathematics concerned with points, lines, shapes, and the space they occupy, from flat figures to solids. This course moves from the basic undefined terms through angles, triangles, the Pythagorean theorem, area and volume, proof, and coordinate methods. The structure is adapted from the Geometry article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: Two distinct points determine exactly one...
questions.explanation: Through any two distinct points there is exactly one straight line - a basic postulate.

questions.prompt: Two angles are complementary when their measures add to...
questions.explanation: Complementary angles sum to 90 degrees; supplementary angles sum to 180 degrees.

questions.prompt: The three interior angles of any triangle add up to...
questions.explanation: The triangle angle-sum is always 180 degrees.

questions.prompt: In a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, the Pythagorean theorem says...
questions.explanation: The squares of the two legs add to the square of the hypotenuse.

questions.prompt: The area of a rectangle with length L and width W is...
questions.explanation: Area is length times width; 2*(L + W) is the perimeter.

questions.prompt: When two lines cross, the angles opposite each other are called...
questions.explanation: Vertical angles sit opposite the crossing and are always equal in measure.

questions.prompt: The circumference of a circle with radius r is...
questions.explanation: Circumference is 2*pi*r; pi*r^2 is the area.

questions.prompt: The volume of a rectangular box (prism) with dimensions l, w, h is...
questions.explanation: Volume of a box is the product of its three dimensions; 2*(l*w + w*h + l*h) is its surface area.

lessons.title: Points, lines, planes, segments, and angles
lessons.grammar_note: A line extends forever in both directions; a segment has two endpoints; a ray has one endpoint and goes on forever the other way - keep the three straight.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name and sketch the basic building blocks of geometry - points, lines, planes, segments, rays, and angles - and measure and classify an angle in degrees. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, how many lines pass through two distinct points? By the end you will be able to add segment lengths along a line, add angles that share a side, and sort any angle as acute, right, obtuse, or straight.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Geometry starts with three undefined terms that we describe rather than define. A point marks a position and has no size. A line is a straight path of points that extends forever in both directions; through any two distinct points there is exactly one line. A plane is a flat surface that extends forever in every direction, like an endless tabletop. From these we build the rest. A line segment is the part of a line between two endpoints, and it has a definite length. A ray starts at one endpoint and extends forever in a single direction. An angle is formed by two rays that share an endpoint called the vertex; we measure how far one ray is turned from the other in degrees, from 0 up to 360. A right angle measures 90 degrees, an acute angle is less than 90 degrees, an obtuse angle is between 90 and 180 degrees, and a straight angle is exactly 180 degrees. These simple pieces combine into every figure you will meet.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Consider points A and B. The segment AB is everything between them, including the endpoints, and its length is written AB. If A and B are 7 units apart, then AB = 7. The ray AB starts at A and passes through B forever; the ray BA starts at B and heads the other way - they are different rays. Now take three points A, B, and C with B between A and C, where AB = 3 and BC = 5. By the segment addition idea, AC = AB + BC = 3 + 5 = 8. For angles, suppose ray OP and ray OQ share vertex O and the angle POQ measures 40 degrees. If ray OR continues so that angle QOR = 50 degrees and the two angles sit side by side, then angle POR = 40 + 50 = 90 degrees, a right angle. Finally, classify a 120 degree angle: since it is between 90 and 180 degrees, it is obtuse.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) How many lines pass through two distinct points? 2) Points P, Q, R lie on a line with Q between the others; if PQ = 4 and QR = 6, find PR. 3) Classify a 90 degree angle. 4) Classify a 35 degree angle. 5) An angle measures 160 degrees - acute, right, or obtuse? 6) Name the shared endpoint of the two rays of an angle. Answers: 1) Exactly one. 2) PR = 4 + 6 = 10. 3) A right angle. 4) Acute, since 35 is less than 90. 5) Obtuse, since 160 is between 90 and 180. 6) The vertex.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating ray AB and ray BA as the same thing - they start at different endpoints and point opposite ways. Mistake: calling a segment a line; a line has no endpoints and never stops, while a segment is bounded. Mistake: reading an angle as obtuse when it is really more than 180 degrees - obtuse tops out just under 180 degrees. Exit: (a) What do we call two rays sharing an endpoint? (b) A segment has how many endpoints? (c) Is a 75 degree angle acute or obtuse? Answers: an angle; two endpoints; acute, because 75 is less than 90 degrees.

lessons.title: Angle relationships and parallel lines cut by a transversal
lessons.grammar_note: Complementary angles add to 90 degrees, supplementary angles add to 180 degrees - 'c' comes before 's' just as 90 comes before 180.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Find complements and supplements, use vertical angles, and chase unknown angles through a diagram of two parallel lines cut by a transversal. Warm-up: if two angles sit next to each other on a straight line, what must their measures add to? By the end you will spot corresponding, alternate interior, alternate exterior, and co-interior angle pairs and use them to solve for a missing angle.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Angles come in named pairs. Two angles are complementary when their measures add to 90 degrees, and supplementary when they add to 180 degrees. When two straight lines cross, they form two pairs of vertical angles - the angles opposite each other - and vertical angles are always equal. The two angles next to each other on a straight line are supplementary, since together they form a straight angle of 180 degrees. Now draw two parallel lines and a third line, called a transversal, that cuts across both. Eight angles appear, and they fall into tidy groups. Corresponding angles, in matching positions at each crossing, are equal. Alternate interior angles, on opposite sides of the transversal and between the parallel lines, are equal. Alternate exterior angles, on opposite sides but outside, are equal too. Co-interior angles, on the same side between the lines, are supplementary. These equalities let you chase an unknown angle across a whole figure once a single angle is known.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: If an angle is 35 degrees, its complement is 90 - 35 = 55 degrees and its supplement is 180 - 35 = 145 degrees. Two lines cross and one angle measures 110 degrees; the angle vertical to it is also 110 degrees, while each neighboring angle is 180 - 110 = 70 degrees. Now two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, and one angle at the top crossing is 75 degrees. The corresponding angle at the bottom crossing is also 75 degrees. The alternate interior angle is 75 degrees as well. The co-interior angle on the same side is 180 - 75 = 105 degrees. As a chase: if angle 1 = 65 degrees and angle 2 is co-interior to it, then angle 2 = 115 degrees, and the angle vertical to angle 2 is also 115 degrees.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Find the complement of a 28 degree angle. 2) Find the supplement of a 90 degree angle. 3) Two lines cross; one angle is 140 degrees - what is its vertical angle? 4) Parallel lines are cut by a transversal; a corresponding angle to a 50 degree angle measures what? 5) Co-interior angles: if one is 70 degrees, what is the other? 6) Can two angles be both complementary and equal? Answers: 1) 90 - 28 = 62 degrees. 2) 180 - 90 = 90 degrees. 3) 140 degrees, since vertical angles are equal. 4) 50 degrees. 5) 180 - 70 = 110 degrees. 6) Yes - two 45 degree angles.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: swapping complementary and supplementary; complementary sums to 90 degrees, supplementary to 180 degrees. Mistake: assuming the transversal rules work for any two lines - they hold only when the two cut lines are parallel. Mistake: thinking vertical angles are supplementary; they are equal, while the adjacent pair is supplementary. Exit: (a) Two angles add to 180 degrees - what are they called? (b) Alternate interior angles on parallel lines are equal or supplementary? (c) The supplement of 120 degrees is what? Answers: supplementary; equal; 180 - 120 = 60 degrees.

lessons.title: Triangles: classification and the angle-sum
lessons.grammar_note: Classify a triangle two ways at once - by its sides (scalene, isosceles, equilateral) and by its angles (acute, right, obtuse).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Classify a triangle by its sides and by its angles, use the triangle angle-sum to find a missing angle, and apply the exterior angle theorem. Warm-up: if a triangle has angles of 40 degrees and 75 degrees, what is the third angle? By the end you will know why the three angles always total 180 degrees and how an exterior angle relates to the two interior angles far from it.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A triangle is a closed figure with three straight sides and three angles. We sort triangles two ways. By sides: a scalene triangle has three different side lengths, an isosceles triangle has at least two equal sides, and an equilateral triangle has all three sides equal. By angles: an acute triangle has all three angles less than 90 degrees, a right triangle has one 90 degree angle, and an obtuse triangle has one angle greater than 90 degrees. The single most useful fact is the triangle angle-sum: the three interior angles of any triangle always add to 180 degrees. A quick way to see it is to imagine tearing off the three corners and fitting them together along a straight line. A close partner is the exterior angle theorem: an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it (the remote interior angles). Because an equilateral triangle has three equal angles summing to 180 degrees, each of its angles is 60 degrees.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A triangle has angles 40 degrees and 75 degrees; the third is 180 - 40 - 75 = 65 degrees. A triangle with sides 5, 5, and 8 has two equal sides, so it is isosceles; the two angles opposite the equal sides are equal. A triangle with a 90 degree angle and legs 3 and 4 is a right triangle. For the exterior angle theorem: if a triangle has remote interior angles of 50 degrees and 60 degrees, the exterior angle at the third vertex is 50 + 60 = 110 degrees, and the interior angle there is 180 - 110 = 70 degrees - which checks, since 50 + 60 + 70 = 180. An equilateral triangle has each angle equal to 180 / 3 = 60 degrees. An isosceles triangle with a 40 degree apex angle has base angles of (180 - 40) / 2 = 70 degrees each.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A triangle has angles 30 degrees and 90 degrees; find the third. 2) Classify a triangle with sides 6, 6, 6 by its sides. 3) Classify a triangle with a 100 degree angle by its angles. 4) The base angles of an isosceles triangle are 55 degrees each; find the apex angle. 5) An exterior angle is 120 degrees; what do its two remote interior angles sum to? 6) Can a triangle have two right angles? Answers: 1) 180 - 30 - 90 = 60 degrees. 2) Equilateral. 3) Obtuse. 4) 180 - 55 - 55 = 70 degrees. 5) 120 degrees. 6) No - two 90 degree angles already total 180 degrees, leaving nothing for the third.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting that the angle-sum is always 180 degrees, not 360 degrees - that is the sum for a quadrilateral. Mistake: calling every triangle with two equal sides equilateral; equilateral needs all three equal, while two equal makes it isosceles. Mistake: thinking a right triangle cannot be isosceles - a 45-45-90 triangle is both. Exit: (a) The three angles of a triangle add to what? (b) Each angle of an equilateral triangle measures what? (c) A triangle with all three sides different is called what? Answers: 180 degrees; 60 degrees; scalene.

questions.prompt: Two angles are supplementary when their measures add to...
questions.explanation: Supplementary angles sum to 180 degrees; complementary angles sum to 90 degrees.

questions.prompt: When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, a pair of alternate interior angles are...
questions.explanation: Alternate interior angles on parallel lines are equal in measure.

questions.prompt: A triangle has angles of 50 degrees and 60 degrees. The third angle is...
A triangle whose three sides all have the same length is called...
questions.explanation: All three equal sides make it equilateral, and all three angles are 60 degrees.

questions.prompt: When two straight lines intersect, each pair of vertical angles is...
questions.explanation: Vertical angles are equal; the adjacent pair, not the vertical pair, is supplementary.

questions.prompt: An exterior angle of a triangle equals...
options: the sum of the two remote interior angles
questions.explanation: The exterior angle theorem: an exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it.

lessons.title: Congruence, similarity, and the Pythagorean theorem
lessons.grammar_note: Congruent means same shape and same size; similar means same shape but possibly different size - similar figures have equal angles and sides in a fixed ratio.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell congruent figures from similar ones, name the triangle congruence shortcuts, use a scale factor, and apply the Pythagorean theorem to find a missing side. Warm-up: a triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 and one with sides 6, 8, 10 - same shape or same size? By the end you will find the hypotenuse or a missing leg of a right triangle and test whether a triangle is right-angled at all.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Two figures are congruent when one can be laid exactly on top of the other - same shape and same size, so matching sides and matching angles are equal. For triangles, you do not need all six measurements to prove congruence; shortcuts like SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the angle between them), ASA (two angles and the side between them), and AAS settle it. Two figures are similar when they have the same shape but not necessarily the same size: matching angles are equal, and matching sides are all in the same ratio, called the scale factor. For triangles, showing two pairs of angles are equal (AA) is enough for similarity. The Pythagorean theorem links the sides of a right triangle: if the legs are a and b and the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) is c, then a^2 + b^2 = c^2. It holds only for right triangles, and its converse is true too - if a^2 + b^2 = c^2, the triangle has a right angle. These tools let you find missing lengths and distances everywhere.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Congruence: two triangles each with sides 3, 4, 5 are congruent by SSS. Similarity: a triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 and one with sides 6, 8, 10 are similar with scale factor 2, since 6/3 = 8/4 = 10/5 = 2. If a 4-unit-tall post casts a 3-unit shadow while a tree casts a 15-unit shadow at the same time, the similar triangles give tree height / 15 = 4 / 3, so the tree is 20 units tall. Pythagorean theorem: a right triangle with legs 6 and 8 has hypotenuse c where c^2 = 6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100, so c = sqrt(100) = 10. Missing leg: if the hypotenuse is 13 and one leg is 5, the other leg b satisfies b^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144, so b = sqrt(144) = 12. Converse: sides 9, 12, 15 satisfy 81 + 144 = 225 = 15^2, so it is a right triangle.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Triangles with sides 5, 12, 13 and 5, 12, 13 are congruent by which rule? 2) Are triangles with sides 2, 3, 4 and 4, 6, 8 similar? Give the scale factor. 3) Find the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 9 and 12. 4) A right triangle has hypotenuse 10 and one leg 6; find the other leg. 5) Do sides 7, 24, 25 form a right triangle? 6) Two triangles share two equal pairs of angles; are they similar? Answers: 1) SSS. 2) Yes, scale factor 2. 3) sqrt(81 + 144) = sqrt(225) = 15. 4) sqrt(100 - 36) = sqrt(64) = 8. 5) 49 + 576 = 625 = 25^2, yes. 6) Yes, by AA.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using the Pythagorean theorem on a triangle that is not right-angled - it holds only for right triangles. Mistake: confusing congruent and similar; congruent figures are the same size, similar figures only share shape. Mistake: pairing a leg with the hypotenuse in the formula; c is always the longest side, opposite the right angle. Exit: (a) In a^2 + b^2 = c^2, which side is c? (b) Similar triangles have sides in what relationship? (c) A triangle with sides 8, 15, 17 - is it right? Answers: the hypotenuse, opposite the right angle; a fixed ratio, the same scale factor; yes, since 64 + 225 = 289 = 17^2.

lessons.title: Perimeter, area, circumference, quadrilaterals, and polygons
lessons.grammar_note: Perimeter is a length (add the sides); area is a surface (square units) - do not mix the two.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Find the perimeter and area of common polygons, the circumference and area of a circle, and the angle sums of quadrilaterals and other polygons. Warm-up: what is the perimeter of an 8 by 5 rectangle, and what is its area? By the end you will apply the right formula for rectangles, squares, triangles, trapezoids, and circles, and compute the interior angle sum of any polygon.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The perimeter of a polygon is the total distance around it - just add the side lengths. Area measures the surface a flat figure covers, in square units. A rectangle of length L and width W has perimeter 2*(L + W) and area L*W. A square of side s has perimeter 4*s and area s^2. A triangle with base b and height h has area (1/2)*b*h. A parallelogram has area base*height, and a trapezoid with parallel sides a and b and height h has area (1/2)*(a + b)*h. For a circle of radius r, the distance around is the circumference C = 2*pi*r, and the area is A = pi*r^2, where pi is about 3.14. Quadrilaterals are four-sided polygons and form a family: a square is a special rectangle, a rectangle is a special parallelogram, and so on. The interior angles of any quadrilateral add to 360 degrees. More generally, a polygon with n sides has interior angles summing to (n - 2)*180 degrees, so a pentagon totals 540 degrees and a hexagon totals 720 degrees.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A rectangle 8 by 5 has perimeter 2*(8 + 5) = 26 and area 8*5 = 40 square units. A square of side 6 has perimeter 4*6 = 24 and area 6^2 = 36. A triangle with base 10 and height 4 has area (1/2)*10*4 = 20. A trapezoid with parallel sides 6 and 10 and height 3 has area (1/2)*(6 + 10)*3 = (1/2)*16*3 = 24. A circle of radius 5 has circumference 2*pi*5 = 10*pi, about 31.4, and area pi*5^2 = 25*pi, about 78.5. Angle sums: a quadrilateral totals 360 degrees, so if three angles are 80, 90, and 100 degrees, the fourth is 360 - 270 = 90 degrees. A pentagon has interior angles summing to (5 - 2)*180 = 540 degrees, so a regular pentagon has each angle equal to 540 / 5 = 108 degrees.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Find the perimeter and area of a 7 by 3 rectangle. 2) Find the area of a triangle with base 12 and height 5. 3) Find the circumference and area of a circle with radius 4 (leave pi in). 4) The interior angles of a hexagon sum to what? 5) Three angles of a quadrilateral are 70, 110, and 95 degrees; find the fourth. 6) Each interior angle of a regular hexagon measures what? Answers: 1) Perimeter 2*(7 + 3) = 20; area 7*3 = 21. 2) (1/2)*12*5 = 30. 3) Circumference 2*pi*4 = 8*pi; area pi*4^2 = 16*pi. 4) (6 - 2)*180 = 720 degrees. 5) 360 - 275 = 85 degrees. 6) 720 / 6 = 120 degrees.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reporting perimeter in square units or area in plain units; perimeter is a length, area is a surface. Mistake: forgetting the (1/2) in the triangle area formula. Mistake: mixing up the circumference (2*pi*r) and the area (pi*r^2) of a circle. Exit: (a) What is the area of a circle of radius r? (b) The interior angles of a polygon with n sides sum to what? (c) A square of side 9 has what perimeter? Answers: pi*r^2; (n - 2)*180 degrees; 4*9 = 36.

lessons.title: Surface area and volume of solids
lessons.grammar_note: Surface area is the total outside area (square units); volume is the space inside (cubic units) - watch the units.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Find the surface area and volume of prisms, cubes, cylinders, cones, and spheres, and keep square and cubic units straight. Warm-up: what is the volume of a box measuring 4 by 3 by 2? By the end you will use base-area-times-height for prisms and cylinders, the one-third rule for cones, and the sphere formulas, leaving pi in for exact answers.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Solids are three-dimensional figures, and we measure two things about them. Surface area is the total area of all the outside faces, in square units. Volume is the amount of space inside, in cubic units. A rectangular prism (a box) with dimensions l, w, h has volume l*w*h and surface area 2*(l*w + w*h + l*h). A cube of side s has volume s^3 and surface area 6*s^2. A cylinder with radius r and height h has volume pi*r^2*h (the circular base area times the height) and surface area 2*pi*r^2 + 2*pi*r*h. A cone with the same radius and height holds exactly one third of the matching cylinder: its volume is (1/3)*pi*r^2*h. A sphere of radius r has volume (4/3)*pi*r^3 and surface area 4*pi*r^2. A handy pattern: prisms and cylinders use base area times height, while cones and pyramids use one third of that. Keep pi as pi for exact answers, and use about 3.14 when you need a number.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A box 4 by 3 by 2 has volume 4*3*2 = 24 cubic units and surface area 2*(4*3 + 3*2 + 4*2) = 2*(12 + 6 + 8) = 2*26 = 52 square units. A cube of side 5 has volume 5^3 = 125 and surface area 6*5^2 = 150. A cylinder with radius 3 and height 10 has volume pi*3^2*10 = 90*pi, about 282.7. A cone with radius 3 and height 10 has volume (1/3)*pi*3^2*10 = 30*pi, exactly one third of that cylinder. A sphere of radius 6 has volume (4/3)*pi*6^3 = (4/3)*pi*216 = 288*pi and surface area 4*pi*6^2 = 144*pi. Doubling a cube's side from 2 to 4 multiplies its volume by 2^3 = 8, since 2^3 = 8 goes to 4^3 = 64.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Find the volume of a box 5 by 4 by 3. 2) Find the surface area of a cube of side 2. 3) Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 2 and height 7 (leave pi in). 4) Find the volume of a cone with radius 6 and height 4. 5) Find the volume of a sphere of radius 3. 6) Find the surface area of a sphere of radius 5. Answers: 1) 5*4*3 = 60 cubic units. 2) 6*2^2 = 24 square units. 3) pi*2^2*7 = 28*pi. 4) (1/3)*pi*6^2*4 = (1/3)*pi*144 = 48*pi. 5) (4/3)*pi*3^3 = (4/3)*pi*27 = 36*pi. 6) 4*pi*5^2 = 100*pi.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: giving volume in square units or surface area in cubic units; volume is cubic, surface area is square. Mistake: dropping the (1/3) for a cone, which turns it into a cylinder. Mistake: using the diameter where the formula wants the radius - the radius is half the diameter. Exit: (a) What is the volume of a cylinder with radius r and height h? (b) A cone has what fraction of the volume of the cylinder with the same base and height? (c) The volume of a cube of side 3 is what? Answers: pi*r^2*h; one third; 3^3 = 27 cubic units.

items.translation: a location in space with no size - no length, width, or height
items.example: The sharp tip of a pencil suggests a point.

items.translation: the part of a line between two endpoints, with a definite length
items.example: The straight edge of a ruler models a line segment.

items.translation: a part of a line with one endpoint that extends forever in one direction
items.example: A beam of light from a single source behaves like a ray.

items.translation: the common endpoint where two rays or two sides meet to form an angle
items.example: Each corner of a square is a vertex.

items.translation: having exactly the same size and shape, so one figure fits perfectly on the other
items.example: Two tiles cut from the same mold are congruent.

items.translation: having the same shape but not necessarily the same size, with sides in a fixed ratio
items.example: A photo and its enlargement are similar.

items.translation: the side opposite the right angle in a right triangle, always the longest side
items.example: In a 3-4-5 right triangle the hypotenuse is 5.

items.translation: meeting at a right angle of 90 degrees
items.example: The two axes of a coordinate grid are perpendicular.

lessons.title: Geometric proof, deductive reasoning, and coordinate geometry
lessons.grammar_note: A proof moves from given facts to a conclusion by reasons; on the coordinate plane, distance uses the Pythagorean theorem and the midpoint averages the coordinates.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Follow a short deductive argument, read a two-column proof, and use the distance and midpoint formulas on the coordinate plane. Warm-up: what is the distance from the point (0, 0) to the point (3, 4)? By the end you will justify a conclusion with a stated reason, tell a postulate from a theorem, and use coordinates to measure and locate the middle of a segment.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Geometry is not just measuring - it is proving. Deductive reasoning starts from accepted facts and reaches a conclusion that must follow. We build on undefined terms, definitions, postulates (statements accepted without proof, such as 'through two points there is exactly one line'), and theorems (statements proved from the rest). A common format is the two-column proof: each statement sits beside the reason that justifies it, step by step, from the givens to the goal. Coordinate geometry brings algebra to this by placing figures on the xy-plane. Two key formulas come straight from the Pythagorean theorem and from averaging. The distance between points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2), because the horizontal and vertical gaps are the legs of a right triangle. The midpoint of the segment joining them is ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2) - just the average of the x-values and the average of the y-values. With these you can prove that a figure is, say, a parallelogram, using numbers instead of a picture.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Distance: from (1, 2) to (4, 6), the gaps are 4 - 1 = 3 and 6 - 2 = 4, so d = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5. Midpoint of the same segment: ((1 + 4)/2, (2 + 6)/2) = (2.5, 4). From (0, 0) to (6, 8): d = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10, and the midpoint is (3, 4). A short deductive chain: given that angle A and angle B are vertical angles, we conclude angle A = angle B, with the reason 'vertical angles are equal.' A two-column snippet: Statement 1, 'AB = CD' (reason: given); Statement 2, 'CD = EF' (reason: given); Statement 3, 'AB = EF' (reason: things equal to the same thing are equal to each other). To test a parallelogram, show both pairs of opposite sides have equal length using the distance formula.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Find the distance from (2, 1) to (2, 7). 2) Find the distance from (0, 0) to (9, 12). 3) Find the midpoint of (3, 5) and (7, 9). 4) Find the midpoint of (-2, 4) and (6, -4). 5) What reason justifies concluding two vertical angles are equal? 6) If AB = CD and CD = GH, what can you conclude and why? Answers: 1) sqrt(0 + 36) = 6. 2) sqrt(81 + 144) = sqrt(225) = 15. 3) ((3 + 7)/2, (5 + 9)/2) = (5, 7). 4) ((-2 + 6)/2, (4 + (-4))/2) = (2, 0). 5) Vertical angles are equal. 6) AB = GH, because things equal to the same thing are equal to each other.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: adding the coordinates in the distance formula instead of subtracting; you need the differences x2 - x1 and y2 - y1. Mistake: subtracting in the midpoint formula - the midpoint averages, so you add and divide by 2. Mistake: treating a postulate as something that needs proof; postulates are accepted starting points, while theorems are proved. Exit: (a) Write the distance formula between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2). (b) What is the midpoint of (0, 0) and (10, 4)? (c) A statement accepted without proof is called what? Answers: sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2); (5, 2); a postulate.
